big_idea: Regret isn't a mistake to avoid, it's a universal, valuable emotion that, when examined rather than suppressed, reveals what people truly value and can be converted into better future decisions.

tool.label: The Four Core Regrets Framework
tool.text: Pink's analysis of tens of thousands of regrets worldwide finds they cluster into four categories: Foundation regrets (failing to do the steady work), Boldness regrets (not taking a chance), Moral regrets (choosing wrong over right in an ethical moment), and Connection regrets (letting a relationship lapse without reaching out). Each maps to a core human need, stability, growth, goodness, and love, so naming which type a regret falls into clarifies what to actually change.

ideas.title: No regrets is bad advice
ideas.text: Suppressing or denying regret forfeits its value as a signal of what matters.

ideas.title: Regret is an upward counterfactual
ideas.text: Imagining a better alternative past deliberately makes you feel worse now so you perform better later.

ideas.title: Four regret categories map to four core needs
A three-step process for using regret productively
ideas.text: Self-disclosure, self-compassion, and self-distancing, analyzing it as an advisor would, then extracting a lesson.

ideas.title: Regrets of inaction outlast regrets of action
ideas.text: Over time people regret chances not taken more than mistakes made, because inaction leaves the what-if unresolved.

ideas.title: Regret is nearly universal
ideas.text: Large surveys find the vast majority of people report regret regularly.

try_it: Write down one specific regret in a few sentences, as if describing it to a friend, then name which of the four categories it fits.
For one connection regret, send a specific, low-stakes message this week to the person you've lost touch with.
Pick one recurring foundation regret and commit to one small, concrete weekly habit that addresses it.
Next time you feel regret, reframe the question from why did I do that to what would I tell a friend in this situation.
best_for: Anyone facing a decision point who wants a structured way to learn from past choices
Leaders and coaches wanting a research-backed vocabulary for reflection
less_useful: Readers wanting a purely tactical business framework rather than a psychology-and-research narrative
Those in acute grief or crisis, for whom the reflective exercises may feel premature
